name: Speed
description: Speed is a frantic two-player shedding card game where players race to get rid of all their cards onto two central piles. Play is simultaneous and real-time. Cards can be played if they are one rank higher or lower (e.g., 6 on 5, or 6 on 7) than the card on the pile. There are no turns. The first player to exhaust their hand and draw pile shouts 'Speed!' to win.

overview.description: Speed is a frantic two-player shedding card game where players race to get rid of all their cards onto two central piles. Play is simultaneous and real-time. Cards can be played if they are one rank higher or lower (e.g., 6 on 5, or 6 on 7) than the card on the pile. There are no turns. The first player to exhaust their hand and draw pile shouts 'Speed!' to win.

history.origins: Speed is an American shedding game of the competitive patience family, related to Spit. It developed in the 20th century as a quicker, simpler variant and is widely played in schools and homes in the United States; it has regional names such as Super-spit, Spit 2, and Rush.
history.cultural: A test of hand-eye coordination more than strategy.
history.evolution: The rule 'Jokers are Wild' was added in some circles to reduce stalemates.

setup.deck: Standard 52-card Anglo-American deck; the full pack is used and dealt between the two players (five to hand, 15 to stock each, and two center piles of six).
setup.dealing: Each player is dealt five cards to form a hand and 15 cards face down to the side as a draw pile. Two six-card piles are then dealt in the center, face down.

rules.objective: Be the first player to play off all of your cards (hand and stock) onto the two center piles; the winner says Speed! to claim the win.
rules.gameplay: Play is simultaneous with no turns. Players flip one face-down center card each to start. Each may play from hand onto either center pile when the card is one rank above, one below, or the same as the top of that pile; only one card at a time. Ace and two may be placed on each other (looping). When hand drops below five cards, draw from your stock to refill to five until stock is empty. When neither can play, both simultaneously flip one card from their side pile onto the center piles. When a player runs out of cards they say Speed! and win.
keyRules: Play one card at a time onto either center pile; rank must be one higher, one lower, or same as the top card.
Refill hand from stock to five cards whenever hand has fewer than five.
When stuck, both players flip one card from side pile onto center; if side piles empty, shuffle center stacks as new side piles.

strategy.basic: Don't think, just play. Scan both piles constantly. If you have a run (5, 6, 7), arrange them in your hand so you can slam them down in one motion.
strategy.intermediate: Blocking: If you see your opponent hesitating with a card, play on that pile to change the number and mess them up. If you have doubles (two 6s), play one on a 5, wait for opponent to play 7? No, play 6 on 5, then play 7 on 6? Speed is key.
strategy.advanced: Memory: Use your peripheral vision to see what the opponent is holding if they are sloppy. If they have mostly high cards, play low cards to keep the piles in low numbers.
tips: Use one hand for playing, one for drawing (or one hand for everything if rules are strict).

variations.name: Jokers as wild
variations.description: Jokers may be played as any rank; when played they act as the rank played on. A joker cannot be the last card played.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Variant only changes deck usage and wild rules; no engine constant overrides needed.

variations.name: Three- or four-hand Speed
variations.description: With three players, each gets five side-pile cards and three face-down center cards; remainder dealt as draw piles. With four players often two decks are used.
variations.emptyOverridesReason: Player-count and deal differ; engine overrides could be added when implementing multi-hand support.

scoring.description: Get rid of all your cards first.
scoring.winCondition: Get rid of all your cards first.
